paragraphs: At the start of a shift, calibrate the machine and test chemical temperature. Load film onto the line and monitor the machine as it produces prints. Inspect every print for color casts and scratches, then reject and reprocess defects. Around midday, replenish chemicals and maintain equipment. In the afternoon, perform specialized processes or quality control. Before leaving, clear the area and record losses.

In short: turn light into photographic paper. Tasks include loading film, mixing chemicals, monitoring machines, finding defects, and restoring images. The role uses both hands and eyes to turn captured images into finished products.

The greatest risk to the role is direct replacement by AI and digitalization. Digital photography eliminated most processing demand, while automated processing machines and online printing absorb standard roles, sharply contracting traditional craft work.

No matter how smart machines become, process workers still decide which images deserve fine-art inkjet printing, which old photographs can be restored, and what makes color accurate. People cannot be removed completely from imaging.
In short, the future shortage will not be of people who can press buttons to process film, but of imaging workers who understand technique and calibrate color accurately.
